en: Land heats faster than the ocean during the day, causing warm air to rise and cool sea breezes to rush inland.
Earthworms digest dead leaves and excrete nutrient-rich castings, which naturally fertilize the soil and help plants grow better.
Slightly acidic rainwater dissolves limestone bedrock over thousands of years, carving out massive underground cave systems like the Puerto Princesa Subterranean River.
Plant roots absorb groundwater and release it as water vapor through their leaves, adding significant moisture to the atmosphere for cloud formation.
Jupiter’s massive gravitational pull acts like a cosmic vacuum, attracting and capturing many comets and asteroids before they can reach Earth.
Extreme pressure in the Sun’s core forces hydrogen atoms to fuse together, releasing the massive amounts of heat and light that warm Earth.
The Moon’s gravitational pull continuously tugs on Earth’s oceans, creating a bulge of water that results in regular high and low tides.
When tectonic plates collide, one plate melts into magma that rises to the surface, triggering volcanic eruptions like those at Mayon Volcano.
Warm, moist air rises into the cooler upper atmosphere, causing water vapor to condense into liquid droplets that eventually fall as rain.
Intense heat and extreme pressure deep underground bake and squeeze existing rocks, transforming ordinary limestone into beautiful, hard metamorphic marble.
Earth’s tilted axis causes different hemispheres to receive varying amounts of direct sunlight throughout its yearly orbit, creating the four distinct seasons.
The Sun’s heat evaporates ocean water into pure water vapor, leaving dissolved salts behind to naturally desalinate the water before it falls as rain.
